title: Zophar Tells Job to Repent
overview: Job's third friend, Zophar, harshly accuses Job of empty talk, insists God sees Job's hidden wrongdoing, and promises a restored life if Job turns away from it.

parts.label: A harsh opening (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Zophar is the bluntest friend yet, calling Job a windbag and a mocker and claiming Job says he is spotless, though Job had only denied being a fraud. He wishes God would speak against Job, and adds a line that seems to say Job is getting off lightly; the Hebrew is unclear, so translations differ.

parts.label: God is beyond reach (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: Zophar says God's wisdom is higher than the sky, deeper than the world of the dead, and wider than land or sea. His point is that Job cannot see enough of God's ways to judge how he is being treated.

parts.label: God sees what we miss (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: Zophar pictures God arresting someone and calling a court that no one can stop, because God spots wrongdoing people overlook. Verse 12 is a proverb comparing a foolish person to an untamed wild donkey, but its wording is hard to translate and scholars read it differently.

parts.label: If you turn back (vv. 13-19)
parts.note: Zophar urges Job to pray and put away any wrongdoing in his home, promising his troubles will fade like water that has drained away and his life will shine again. Lifting up his face answers Job's own words in the previous chapter, and the line about many seeking him out literally pictures people stroking his face, a sign of being honored.

parts.label: A warning (v. 20)
parts.note: Zophar ends by saying the wicked look for rescue in vain and their hope slips away like a last breath. It is a pointed hint that Job will share that end if he does not change.

disagreement: Because God later says the friends did not speak rightly about him, Christians differ on how much of Zophar's speech, including its fine lines about God's greatness, should be read as true teaching and how much as a portrait of mistaken thinking.
think: When someone is suffering, what makes an explanation feel like help rather than a verdict?
